A) Yes: St. John’s forces Duke into a substantially higher turnover rate than Duke’s season norms (roughly mid-to-high teens for Duke) and converts those mistakes into enough points that the game is not settled mainly by Duke’s half-court execution.
B) No: Duke largely protects the ball (stays near its low-turnover baseline) and limits St. John’s forced-turnover impact to a level that does not change the possession margin in St. John’s favor.

Can St. John’s win the offensive glass battle enough to offset Duke’s defensive rebounding and shot suppression?
A) Yes: St. John’s offensive rebounding (driven by Ejiofor/Mitchell and their frontcourt crashing) produces a clear second-chance edge and meaningfully increases second-chance points over Duke’s usual defensive rebounding suppression.
B) No: Duke neutralizes the glass (contests misses, limits offensive rebounds/second-chance points) so St. John’s extra possessions do not translate into scoreboard separation.

Can St. John’s interior offense (especially Zuby Ejiofor) generate efficient scoring despite Duke’s size/length and defensive rating profile?
A) Yes: Ejiofor (and the Mitchell/Hopkins frontcourt group) gets enough paint touches and high-quality interior looks to score efficiently and also create for teammates without being largely limited to low-efficiency attempts.
B) No: Duke’s length/shot suppression materially reduces Ejiofor’s efficiency (lower shot-quality frequency and/or higher contest rate), so St. John’s offense settles into a less reliable outcome (more jumpers/less paint production).

Will foul trouble / free-throw rate skew the game toward St. John’s (i.e., St. John’s earns a high number of free throws and uses them to offset any efficiency gap)?
A) Yes: St. John’s draws a high FT volume (near the upper range cited in their notes/season behavior) and converts enough at the line to neutralize Duke’s defensive advantage.
B) No: The whistle stays relatively controlled—St. John’s FT volume is not high enough, so they can’t win through free-throw variance and must outscore Duke with shot efficiency and/or offensive rebounds.

How much does the game script depend on 3-point variance (St. John’s low-to-moderate 3PA profile vs. Duke’s ability to create paint/efficient looks): will either team get unusually above-average perimeter shooting?
A) Yes: One or both teams hit an above-normal share of their perimeter looks (e.g., St. John’s 3s fall at a higher clip than their low attempt-rate usually implies, or Duke’s kickouts/wing 3s remain efficiently converted), swinging expected points.
B) No: Shooting regresses to profile (Duke’s offense stays efficient mainly through paint/boards and controlled shot quality; St. John’s does not receive the 3-point lift needed to compensate for interior/possession deficits).

Is Duke’s offensive execution disrupted early by St. John’s defensive pressure such that Duke can’t consistently run its Boozer-led inside-out half-court offense?
A) Yes: St. John’s pressure and defensive structure deny Duke’s clean interior catches/second-chance rhythm early enough that Duke’s offensive rating drops materially for a sustained stretch.
B) No: Duke settles into its offense—Boozer still functions as the interior hub, and Duke’s paint pressure and kickouts produce consistent scoring even if the game is physical.

In this matchup, will St. John’s be able to win the rebounding battle and generate a meaningfully higher number of second-chance points than Duke?
A) Yes: St. John’s will outrebound Duke (or at least match them) enough to keep offensive rebounds high, producing a clear edge in second-chance points (e.g., roughly +5 or more).
B) No: Duke will win the possession-end of the rebounding battle (at minimum neutralizing offensive rebounds), so St. John’s second-chance points will not be a decisive edge (e.g., 0 to +2).

Which team is more likely to control shooting efficiency against the other’s defensive profile (field/effective FG)?
A) Yes: St. John’s will shoot at or near its profile and avoid Duke driving it into low-efficiency looks—effective FG stays relatively normal (e.g., not dramatically below season baseline).
B) No: Duke’s defense will meaningfully suppress St. John’s efficiency (forcing a large drop in eFG/FGA quality), consistent with Duke’s season-level opponents’ eFG%/3P suppression profile.

Will the turnover matchup tilt toward St. John’s pressure outcomes (more turnovers created than committed), giving St. John’s a turnover-to-points advantage?
A) Yes: St. John’s forces enough turnovers (and converts them) to produce a positive turnover margin with a visible points-off-turnovers edge.
B) No: Duke protects the ball and/or reduces St. John’s ability to disrupt; turnover margin stays neutral to Duke-favored, limiting points off turnovers for St. John’s.

Will Duke’s pace/possession structure limit St. John’s ability to turn stops into fast-break and paint runs?
A) Yes: Duke controls tempo/shot quality so St. John’s cannot consistently build its preferred runouts and fast-break points; fewer transition points occur for St. John’s.
B) No: The game still features enough transition possessions (or stoppage quality that St. John’s converts) that St. John’s fast-break pressure remains a major scoring source.

Will Duke’s offensive scheme (Boozer-centric interior creation + kick-outs) generate at least one stable high-efficiency scoring lane throughout the night?
A) Yes: Duke sustains efficient interior production through Boozer/paint touches such that the offense looks consistently functional (not just sporadic).
B) No: St. John’s frontcourt pressure/physicality disrupts Duke’s interior rhythm enough that Boozer’s efficiency collapses and Duke must rely heavily on lower-efficiency exterior/late-clock outcomes.

Who is more likely to be the ‘free-throw-advantage’ driver given foul-drawing and defensive contact patterns?
A) Yes: St. John’s earns the free-throw volume edge (i.e., repeatedly gets to the line at a higher rate), offsetting any efficiency gap.
B) No: Duke’s defensive discipline/shot contesting reduces foul attempts; St. John’s free throws do not meaningfully outweigh Duke’s ability to score.

Coaching/strategy — Can Scheyer’s in-game adjustments neutralize St. John’s mid-game defensive pressure and possession-style (turnovers/second chances) before it decides the game?
A) Yes: Scheyer makes effective mid-game/halftime adjustments (lineups, matchups, ball-handling/passing options) that reduce St. John’s ability to create turnovers and second-chance possessions.
B) No: St. John’s pressure and rebounding/FT packages remain effective despite adjustments, keeping its preferred possession outcomes intact through key stretches.

Coaching/strategy — Will Pitino be able to tailor rotations and schemes to keep St. John’s best interior creators (Ejiofor + frontcourt) consistently involved without defensive matchup breakdowns?
A) Yes: Pitino’s rotation/matchup choices keep Ejiofor and the frontline productive while preserving defensive integrity against Duke’s inside-out actions.
B) No: Duke’s matchup hunting and length force foul trouble/inefficient minutes or matchup mismatches that blunt St. John’s frontline scoring and/or defensive effectiveness.

Momentum & psychology — If the game reaches a late one-possession or two-possession period, is Duke more likely to execute under pressure based on recent closing evidence?
A) Yes: Duke’s late-game execution (spacing, set offense, clutch stops/FTs) is more reliable, leading to more consistent winning possessions late.
B) No: St. John’s pressure-hardened finishing (late ties, go-ahead moments, clutch plays) will outperform Duke in the final possessions.

Momentum & psychology — Which team is more likely to handle an early scoring run from the opponent without losing offensive structure or committing costly turnovers?
A) Yes: St. John’s absorbs early deficits and responds with defensive pressure bursts that reassert control; early Duke runs don’t create durable separation.
B) No: Duke’s structure withstands early St. John’s runs because of ball security and shot-quality defense; St. John’s can’t sustain enough scoring after initial spurts.

Health & conditioning — Are both teams’ key rotation players available at full capacity (no significant injuries/limitations that would change defensive/offensive roles)?
A) Yes: No meaningful injury/limitation affects primary creators/defenders (Boozer/Evans/Brown/Ngongba for Duke; Ejiofor/Mitchell/Hopkins/Jackson/Darling/Sellers for St. John’s).
B) No: One side has a notable availability or limitation (minutes restriction, injury, or foul-susceptibility) that materially changes rotation effectiveness in the second half.

Health & conditioning — If foul trouble hits a primary frontcourt player, does that team have enough depth to preserve its identity (rebounding defense for Duke; paint/physical scoring for St. John’s)?
A) Yes: The team whose key starter is targeted can absorb the foul-impact with bench/next options without losing defensive rebounding/paint resistance (or interior passing/scoring).
B) No: Foul trouble forces lineup drop-offs that significantly harm that team’s core strengths (glass/paint defense for Duke or frontline scoring/connection for St. John’s).

Historical & situational — How much does coaching/tournament experience advantage actually matter here relative to matchup mechanics?
A) Yes: Experience and proven tournament adjustment capacity (Scheyer’s deep runs; Pitino’s tournament history) meaningfully increases expected execution quality in high-leverage moments.
B) No: Experience effects are secondary; the matchup (rebounding + turnover + efficiency) dominates, so historical tournament pedigree won’t swing the outcome much.

Historical & situational — Is travel/site or tournament context (e.g., neutral court but with specific crowd/venue factors) likely to advantage St. John’s or Duke?
A) Yes: Venue/crowd dynamics (or perceived home-fan distribution like NYC-area proximity) tilt the atmosphere in St. John’s favor, boosting energy and late-game confidence.
B) No: The game is effectively neutral such that crowd effects are negligible; neither team gets a meaningful situational lift beyond their play.

Stylistic clash — Does Duke’s elite defensive rebounding and shot suppression more strongly neutralize St. John’s ‘manufactured possessions’ path than St. John’s can compensate with foul pressure and second chances?
A) Yes: Duke’s profile attacks St. John’s primary leverage points (extra possessions and efficiency), so St. John’s manufactured-possession advantage fails to materialize.
B) No: St. John’s still finds enough offensive rebounds + free throws that its manufactured-possession identity survives, keeping the game within its preferred scoring environment.

Stylistic clash — Does St. John’s pressure/man defense disrupt Duke’s ball movement and create enough scoring opportunities without allowing Duke to exploit mismatch mismatches in the half court?
A) Yes: St. John’s pressure forces Duke into turnovers or uncomfortable possessions, while Duke cannot consistently win the interior-outside reads.
B) No: Duke resists the pressure and then exploits the inevitable openings/mismatch hunting (Boozer as hub + Evans spacing), turning St. John’s defensive aggression into predictable half-court advantages for Duke.

Is Duke’s defensive efficiency (or season-long defense) high enough to reliably suppress St. John’s paint + second-chance production (offensive rebounds/2nd-chance points) in this specific matchup?
A) Yes. Duke’s season-long defensive rating and shot suppression keep St. John’s offensive rebounds/second-chance points near or below its season average.
B) No. St. John’s still wins the offensive rebounding and paint-possession battle at a high rate, generating more second-chance and foul opportunities than Duke can contain.

Does St. John’s force enough turnovers to meaningfully offset Duke’s generally low-turnover offense profile?
A) Yes. St. John’s pressure creates a turnover margin large enough (relative to Duke’s ~low turnover rate) to produce extra possessions and transition points.
B) No. Duke protects the ball too well, limiting St. John’s turnover advantage and starving their transition/extra-possession edge.

Will Cameron Boozer face enough physical/coverage pressure that his efficiency drops substantially below his season norms?
A) Yes. St. John’s frontcourt defense and physicality force Boozer into lower-efficiency looks (fewer high-post catches or lower FG% on touches).
B) No. Boozer remains the hub/beneficiary of matchups, maintaining a near-season efficiency because Duke still gets interior touches despite pressure.

Can Duke win the rebounding battle (especially defensive rebounding and limiting second chances) enough to prevent St. John’s from converting misses into repeat shots?
A) Yes. Duke’s size/length and rebounding suppression keep St. John’s offensive rebound rate close to or below St. John’s effective season values.
B) No. St. John’s offensive rebounding remains a major driver, meaning Duke fails to end possessions with defensive boards frequently enough.

Is St. John’s offensive performance likely to come from its ‘process’ (FTs, offensive rebounds, paint touches) rather than elite three-point variance?
A) Yes. The expected offense is built around offensive boards/FTs/paint attempts; three-point shooting is not the main determinant of success.
B) No. St. John’s success depends heavily on above-expected shooting (including threes), so if shooting regresses, their process edge doesn’t fully carry them.

Will officiating (free-throw rate) swing toward St. John’s style (foul drawing/paint contact) rather than neutralizing it?
A) Yes. Expect a whistle tilt that produces many St. John’s free throws and helps compensate for less efficient field-goal shooting.
B) No. Free-throw attempts stay closer to typical/neutral levels, reducing St. John’s ability to win via contact-driven scoring.

Can Duke keep St. John’s effective field-goal percentage (eFG%) from reaching its best outcomes by contesting shot quality and limiting clean looks?
A) Yes. Duke contests enough perimeter and denies easy interior finishes so St. John’s eFG% stays materially below their peak games.
B) No. St. John’s gets enough high-percentage interior looks and second-chance scores that eFG% rises despite Duke’s defense.

Will Duke be able to generate offensive rebounding points at a rate that matches or exceeds St. John’s defensive resistance on the glass?
A) Yes. Duke’s offensive rebounding (and second-chance scoring) stays a meaningful scoring channel.
B) No. St. John’s secures the glass against Duke sufficiently that Duke loses extra-possessions and second-shot points.

Is Duke’s controlled pace (not too high tempo) a net advantage specifically against St. John’s pressure system?
A) Yes. Slower/controlled possessions reduce the number of opportunities for St. John’s full-court pressure to create turnovers and run-outs.
B) No. Even with Duke’s control, St. John’s half-court pressure/turnover creation still creates enough chaos; pace control doesn’t neutralize the matchup.

Will St. John’s ‘low three-point attempt rate’ remain an advantage if they get enough free throws and paint points, or is it a liability against Duke’s length?
A) Advantage. Low reliance on threes is fine because St. John’s can win with paint drives, offensive boards, and foul pressure.
B) Liability. If shots at the rim are contested and offensive rebounds aren’t there, low three-point attempt volume means they cannot keep up on scoreboard via long-range scoring.

Does St. John’s defensive pressure meaningfully disrupt Duke’s half-court set execution through passing lanes and forcing hurried decisions?
A) Yes. St. John’s pressure forces Duke into low-quality shots or turnovers that break the Boozer-led structure.
B) No. Duke settles into the half court and still runs its inside-out sets efficiently despite pressure.

Will St. John’s be able to contain Duke’s interior-to-kickout sequence (paint pressure leading to kick-outs to wings)?
A) Yes. St. John’s defenses compress the lane and recover to contest kick-outs, limiting rim-to-corner/wide-open threes.
B) No. Duke’s interior creation still draws help and produces open perimeter looks; St. John’s is forced to foul or concede efficient perimeter shots.

Is the matchup at the ‘5/4’ spots (Ejiofor vs Duke frontcourt; Mitchell/Hopkins vs Duke wings/second bodies) likely to create foul trouble for one team?
A) Yes. One side’s bigs (likely St. John’s frontcourt) force enough contact that defensive fouls pile up, producing a FT advantage.
B) No. Foul rates stay manageable; neither team gets a decisive FT edge from frontcourt matchup friction.

Can Duke’s length-based shot contesting reduce St. John’s ability to finish through traffic (especially around the elbow/short roll)?
A) Yes. Duke contests at the level of finishing lanes, lowering rim/short-roll efficiency.
B) No. St. John’s big-to-big connectivity and elbow/low-block touches still produce high-percentage finishes.

Will St. John’s ‘offensive rebound to second-chance points’ conversion rate stay high even when Duke’s defense is elite?
A) Yes. The conversion remains strong; misses continue to become second chances at a high frequency.
B) No. Duke converts defensive stops into controlled possessions and limits second-chance opportunities, reducing conversion.

Does Duke’s late-game adjustment history (rebounding + defensive recalibration after halftime) translate to this opponent’s matchup profile?
A) Yes. Duke’s coaching adjustments neutralize St. John’s pressure/second-chance patterns as the game evolves.
B) No. St. John’s game planning and Pitino adjustments specifically counter Duke’s adjustments, keeping the game in St. John’s preferred problems (chaos/FT/boards).

Is St. John’s defense more effective against ‘finishers’ than against a ‘hub-and-spoke’ interior creator like Boozer?
A) Yes. St. John’s tends to disrupt players who need stable spacing; Boozer still gets enough to operate, so Duke suffers less than expected.
B) No. St. John’s pressure and length deny interior catches effectively enough to break Boozer’s hub role, not just his finishing.

Does St. John’s rely on specific late-game personnel (e.g., Sellers/Hopkins/Darling lineups) in ways that mismatch Duke’s best defensive units?
A) Yes. St. John’s closing units create matchup advantages and can punish Duke’s most reliable defenders late.
B) No. Duke’s defensive lineup depth and switchability allow it to match St. John’s late rotations without losing major segments of the floor.

Is Duke’s effective field-goal creation (eFG%) more robust than St. John’s expected value given St. John’s lower three-point attempt rate?
A) Yes. Duke’s shot quality and inside-out efficiency keeps scoring stable even if St. John’s creates turnovers.
B) No. St. John’s can keep games within a narrow scoring band via FT/boards; when Duke’s efficiency dips, St. John’s still wins the possession math.

Will either team’s shot profile create a high-variance outcome (e.g., Duke’s perimeter shots or St. John’s midrange/paint-dependent finishes) that swings the result?
A) Yes. One team’s perimeter/midrange variance will be decisive, with that team sustaining shooting long enough to win.
B) No. The game stays dominated by process stats (boards, FTs, turnover margin), so shooting variance is not the main driver.

Is Duke’s vulnerability path (stopping size dominance) likely to appear because St. John’s can match physicality and limit offensive rebounding?
A) Yes. St. John’s athletic/physical frontcourt limits Duke’s backboard edge and compresses interior scoring efficiency.
B) No. St. John’s cannot neutralize Duke’s size advantage fully; Duke still wins the physical matchup on rebounds and interior touches.

Is St. John’s vulnerability path (needing toughness in non-turnover possessions) likely to appear because Duke can protect the ball and slow possession swing?
A) Yes. If Duke reduces live-ball turnovers and controls tempo enough, St. John’s cannot generate enough extra possessions to win.
B) No. Even without a huge turnover advantage, St. John’s rebounding and foul pressure still create enough scoring margin.

Do roster-specific matchup height/strength factors (Duke guard size vs St. John’s wings; St. John’s backcourt size vs Duke’s perimeter defenders) predict consistent advantages in isolation or post-ups?
A) Yes. Measurable height/strength mismatches persist, producing repeatable scoring advantages for one team.
B) No. Switches, help defense, and rotations neutralize mismatches enough that post-up/isolation advantages don’t repeat.

Is there any credible injury/availability concern for either team’s top creators/big men (Boozer or Ejiofor/Mitchell/Hopkins) that could materially affect usage?
A) Yes. A key player’s health/availability is limited enough to reduce efficiency, minutes, or aggressiveness.
B) No. Both teams’ primary anchors are healthy enough to play their normal roles and minutes, keeping the baseline matchup intact.

Will foul trouble risk differ between teams because one system is more likely to drive contact (St. John’s) while the other is more likely to contest with length (Duke)?
A) Yes. St. John’s draws enough fouls to produce a late-game foul-shooting advantage (and/or Duke picks up early fouls trying to contest).
B) No. Foul trouble is not a deciding factor; both teams get reasonable whistle outcomes and avoid extended time off the floor.

Can St. John’s reach the foul line at a rate high enough to offset Duke’s shot-quality and defensive rating—i.e., St. John’s draws at least ~28 free throws (or wins FTA margin by a meaningful amount) in the game?
A) Yes: St. John’s draws at least ~28 free throws and/or wins the free-throw attempt margin by 6+ (their “foul pressure + extra possessions” materially shows up on the stat sheet).
B) No: St. John’s draws fewer than ~28 free throws and loses the FTA margin (Duke prevents the whistle and/or forces St. John’s into contested jumpers).

Does St. John’s win the offensive rebounding/second-chance battle against Duke (e.g., offensive rebounds or second-chance points)?
A) Yes: St. John’s finishes with a higher offensive-rebound total (or a clear second-chance points edge, e.g., +6 or more).
B) No: St. John’s fails to win the offensive glass; either Duke wins offensive rebounds outright or the second-chance points margin is neutral/negative for St. John’s.

Is Zuby Ejiofor (and the frontcourt passing/creation he anchors) efficient enough to dominate Duke’s half-court defense—i.e., Ejiofor scores at least ~18 points on acceptable efficiency while also contributing materially (rebounds or assists)?
A) Yes: Ejiofor posts at least ~18 points with strong contribution (e.g., 18+ points and either 8+ rebounds or 4+ assists), indicating Duke can’t suffocate the interior hub.
B) No: Ejiofor is held below ~18 points and/or is limited to inefficient scoring plus low impact (fewer rebounds/assists), indicating Duke successfully crowds his touches.

Does Duke’s interior hub Cameron Boozer maintain efficiency against St. John’s (i.e., Boozer is not forced into low-true-shot attempts by coverage) — say 18+ points and above-baseline efficiency?
A) Yes: Boozer scores 18+ points on solid efficiency (e.g., around 50% FG or better) despite St. John’s pressure/physical play, preserving Duke’s offense through the post/face-up actions.
B) No: Boozer is held under 18 points and/or his efficiency collapses (e.g., ~40–45% FG or worse), showing St. John’s frontcourt defense disrupts the hub.

Can St. John’s force enough turnovers to swing transition/early-possession scoring (not just generate steals in random moments) — e.g., St. John’s creates a sizable turnover advantage?
A) Yes: St. John’s achieves a clear turnover margin win (e.g., forces 6+ more turnovers than they commit) and converts at least modestly into points off turnovers/transition (visible in points-off-turnovers and fast-break points).
B) No: St. John’s turnover creation doesn’t materialize as a margin win (turnover margin is neutral or Duke wins it), limiting transition damage.

Does Duke suppress St. John’s offensive rebounding and foul-draw attempts enough that St. John’s shooting volume/quality stays mediocre (eFG/3PA outcomes)?
A) Yes: Duke keeps St. John’s eFG% at or below roughly mid-range (e.g., ~50% or below) and prevents clean rim/paint drives such that St. John’s can’t lean on its usual paint/extra-trip formula.
B) No: St. John’s converts at a much higher rate than its typical efficiency profile (higher eFG% and/or a strong paint/FT share), indicating Duke’s defensive suppression didn’t work.

Does Duke’s defense limit St. John’s 3-point creation volume enough (given St. John’s is not a high-3PA team, the key is whether they still get makeable looks) — e.g., St. John’s makes few enough threes and/or gets limited attempts?
A) Yes: St. John’s 3-point attempts and makes are kept low enough that the defense effectively removes a relief valve (e.g., St. John’s makes 4 or fewer threes).
B) No: St. John’s gets enough perimeter success (e.g., 5+ threes made) or enough attempt volume that Duke’s interior strategy is forced to “help and leak.”

Is the game script controlled by Duke’s pace/shot selection rather than St. John’s pressure-to-extra-possessions plan?
A) Yes: Duke controls possessions—either by lowering total possessions or by ensuring the points-per-possession stay favorable (shot clock/set-play dominance rather than chaos).
B) No: St. John’s turns the game into a possession-rich, chaotic contest (turnovers + offensive rebounding + free throws) that increases effective possessions and raises St. John’s variance path.

Does officiating (foul call distribution, especially late-game) favor the FT-heavy style—i.e., St. John’s gets a demonstrably favorable late foul/FT sequence?
A) Yes: In late game (e.g., final 10 minutes), St. John’s receives a disproportionate share of defensive fouls/free-throw opportunities that materially changes possession totals or closing margins.
B) No: Fouls/FT opportunities are balanced or favor Duke; late-game officiating does not create the “whistle equity” St. John’s relies on.

Are Duke’s late-game execution and shot-making “floor” performances present (e.g., Duke wins key possessions in the final ~6 minutes) rather than collapsing into the upset-friendly finishing range?
A) Yes: Duke wins the late-game possession battle (final-minute FG/FT efficiency and defensive stops), preventing St. John’s from completing its pressure/FT climb.
B) No: Duke’s late possessions regress (turnovers, missed front-end FTs, or poor shot quality), placing St. John’s on the free-throw/chaos path to the upset.

Do St. John’s perimeter guards (e.g., Ian Jackson/Darling) hit enough shot-making to keep Duke from doubling/crowding the paint (i.e., at least modest made threes or effective midrange creation)?
A) Yes: Backcourt/wing creators hit enough jump shots or midrange to punish Duke when help arrives (e.g., multiple makes from outside that prevent interior camping).
B) No: Perimeter production is limited (few or no meaningful made jumpers), allowing Duke to stay home more often and keep Boozer isolated effectively.

Are both teams healthy enough that their primary lineups match the scouting assumptions (no major minutes restriction for key creators/defenders)?
A) Yes: No significant player-health issues; primary rotation minutes (Boozer, Evans, Ejiofor, Demary/Jackson/Darling) are near their normal levels and performance isn’t visibly compromised.
B) No: At least one key player is limited (minutes restriction or clearly subpar play), materially changing matchup dynamics.

Home-court/arena effects are materially favorable to St. John’s—i.e., game location, crowd distribution, or travel fatigue affects Duke’s rhythm (visible via shooting/turnovers deviations).
A) Yes: The environment/timing disproportionately favors St. John’s (crowd + travel + routine differences), and Duke’s execution shows measurable disruption (higher turnovers, worse shooting).
B) No: Arena effects are not decisive; both teams’ execution looks typical and the stat lines don’t show meaningful “environment” disruption.

Will Duke win the possession-ending “glass” battle (at least a slight edge in total rebounding/second-chance possession generation) in the specific game?
A) Duke outrebounds St. John’s and/or records a clear second-chance advantage (more offensive rebounds leading to points) that materially drives the scoring margin.
B) St. John’s wins the rebound/second-chance possession battle (at or above even rebounding with more second-chance points), neutralizing one of Duke’s main identity edges.

Will turnover outcomes favor Duke (Duke’s turnover differential is positive in-game) despite St. John’s pressure/forcing style?
A) Duke commits fewer turnovers than St. John’s forces (positive net turnover differential for Duke).
B) St. John’s wins the turnover battle in-game (Duke commits at least as many or more turnovers; net turnover differential favors St. John’s).

Will Duke’s half-court offense convert efficiently—specifically, will their effective field-goal percentage be above St. John’s in-game?
A) Duke outshoots St. John’s in effective terms (Duke’s in-game eFG% is higher).
B) St. John’s limits Duke’s efficiency so that St. John’s posts the higher in-game eFG%.

Will St. John’s get to the free-throw line significantly more than Duke (FTr/FT attempts advantage)?
A) St. John’s earns a clear free-throw attempts advantage (more FTAs than Duke), reflecting successful paint pressure/foul-drawing.
B) FT attempts are roughly even or favor Duke; St. John’s does not translate paint pressure into a meaningful free-throw edge.

Will St. John’s keep shot volume from deep low enough that their scoring is driven by interior/paint and second chances rather than perimeter variance?
A) St. John’s takes a low-to-moderate three-point volume and still scores effectively via paint touches/offensive rebounding/FTs (i.e., low 3PA doesn’t hurt them).
B) St. John’s ends up relying on perimeter shooting (high enough 3PA that they can fall behind if the shot-making doesn’t land).

Will Duke be able to run their preferred half-court structure through Cameron Boozer as a high-efficiency hub (measured by Boozer’s shot quality/efficiency and contribution to team scoring)?
A) Boozer achieves efficient production and facilitates (team offense looks like a Boozer hub game; Boozer’s scoring efficiency is not suppressed).
B) Boozer’s efficiency is notably suppressed (high effort/low efficiency; limited offensive organizing impact), forcing Duke to rely more on contested jumpers/secondary creation.

Can St. John’s defend Duke’s wings/screens/paint pressure without giving up too many transition stops after misses?
A) St. John’s limits Duke’s ability to turn stops/boards into easy transition points and contested paint looks.
B) St. John’s fails to manage Duke’s transition/second-chance scoring, allowing Duke to repeatedly convert possessions after stops/rebounds.

Does coaching/adjustment during the game produce a clear swing in defensive effectiveness for the eventual winner (e.g., second-half defensive performance gap)?
A) The winning team shows a measurable second-half defensive improvement (opponent scoring/shot quality worsens after adjustments).
B) There is no meaningful defensive swing after adjustments; results are driven more by execution/variance than by tactical mid-game changes.

Will Duke’s defensive scheme limit St. John’s interior passing/creation (Ejiofor-Mitchell-Hopkins elbow/short-roll comfort) over most possessions?
A) St. John’s interior creators are constrained enough that their half-court playmaking advantage is muted (interior passes/entry quality deteriorate).
B) St. John’s interior remains functional; Ejiofor (and frontcourt) still orchestrate a high share of productive half-court possessions.

Will St. John’s defensive pressure actually increase Duke’s turnovers and disrupt rhythm for long enough to flip possession dominance?
A) St. John’s pressure successfully disrupts Duke’s rhythm early/throughout, producing a sustained live-ball mistake/turnover stream.
B) Duke largely settles into offense; pressure does not create a sustained turnover/shot-quality collapse.
